episodes.title: Paul Christiano – We could be 12 months away from AIs that can overthrow the government
episodes.about: Paul Christiano is head of the Alignment Research Center. Previously, he was head of AI safety at the US AI Safety Institute. Before that, he led alignment at OpenAI, where he invented RLHF. He’s recently joined OpenAI’s board (though here he is speaking as a private citizen). Paul thinks that on the current trajectory (absent any slowing down), there is a 1 in 3 chance that we could have superintelligence powerful enough to overthrow the government within a year. (He articulates a concrete scenario). He argues that the labs should pause further algorithmic progress until they can secure their weights and research secrets. Otherwise China could simply steal the superintelligence in the middle of the intelligence explosion, and the labs would no longer be able to slow down even if they saw their models going off the rails. He also explains how AIs will be trained during the intelligence explosion, and why even a system trained entirely inside a data center could still have the capabilities profile such that humans would have very little chance of competing with it or controlling it. And he discusses the plan for alignment - basically, making a superintelligence that actually does what we ask the way we mean it. Fixing reward hacks and building better graders will help up till the next few model generations, but he thinks that no single current approach has better than even odds of letting us control superintelligence. The hope is that the AIs figure out the solution to this problem during the intelligence explosion.
episodes.why: Paul Christiano, who invented RLHF and now heads the Alignment Research Center, puts a 1-in-3 chance on superintelligence that could overthrow the government within a year — and argues labs should pause until their weights are secure.

episodes.title: Building Visual Intelligence — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs
episodes.about: What can a model learn about the world by watching video and listening to it? Black Forest Labs trained FLUX 3 on images, video and audio together. Andreas Blattmann and Dustin Podell join swyx to explain why: a still image shows where a tossed ball is, but video shows how it got there and sound tells you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That is BFL's argument for training on the three signals together — its case for learning visual intelligence from pixels, motion and sound.
episodes.why: Black Forest Labs trained its new FLUX 3 on images, video and audio together; latent-diffusion co-inventor Andreas Blattmann explains what a model learns from motion and sound that a still image cannot teach it.

episodes.title: AI cameras are spotting wildfires before anyone calls 911
episodes.about: A wildfire breaks out in the mountains of Utah. Nobody sees it. Nobody smells smoke. Nobody calls 911. But somehow, a local firefighter knows about it anyway. Which is strange, because someone — or something — had to spot it first. Turns out, it was an AI-powered camera on a mountaintop. And cameras like it are changing who — or what — gets to a wildfire first.
episodes.why: AI-powered cameras on Utah mountaintops are spotting wildfires before anyone calls 911 — a concrete look at who, or what, now gets to a fire first.

episodes.title: How Humans Will Work Alongside AI Agents — With Mike Cannon-Brookes
episodes.about: Mike Cannon-Brookes is the CEO and co-founder of Atlassian, the company behind Jira, Confluence, and Loom. Mike joins Big Technology to discuss how AI is changing work and the software businesses use to get it done, recorded live at Web Summit. Tune in to hear how AI agents will work alongside people, why better models haven’t always translated into productivity gains, and whether AI will eliminate jobs or change them. We also cover model commoditization, competition from OpenAI and Anthropic, and why Mike believes going “headless” is a mistake for software companies.
episodes.why: Atlassian CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes, recorded live at Web Summit, on how agents will work alongside people — and why better models have not yet meant productivity gains.

episodes.title: Replit’s $9B perfect storm, and the winds of “AI psychosis,” with Amjad Masad
episodes.about: A couple of years ago, Replit was flatlining at a few million dollars in annual revenue and running a mostly empty office after a layoff. Today the vibe-coding pioneer is valued at $9 billion, up from $3 billion just six months ago. Recorded live at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco, CEO Amjad Masad joins Bob Safian to ride out the AI storm, revealing what made the turnaround possible, including a slow and steady enterprise bet while competitors poured money into ads, and what it really means to be an AI-first company. He weighs in on what he calls AI psychosis, and says cybersecurity, not AI extinction, is the risk worth focusing on. He also argues that automated software engineering is already safer than human engineering, and describes how that’s changing work inside Replit, where the clatter of mechanical keyboards has given way to whiteboard debates.
episodes.why: Replit CEO Amjad Masad on the vibe-coding company's climb from flatlining to a $9B valuation, what he calls AI psychosis, and why he says automated software engineering is already safer than the human kind.
